catalog_quote: 15. Accent and intonation can only be learnt accurately by ear. The general rule is, that the chief accent falls on the last syllable but one. But prominence is often given to another syllable, which (for whatever reason) to the native mind requires it, by a distinct stress, which affects but does not annul the usual accent. In some cases the gain is obvious in clearness of meaning. The addition of an enclitic syllable, such as -ko, -mo, -wo at the end of a verb, is another cause of change, by drawing the regular accent forward. Moreover, in ordinary rapid speech, the final vowel of a verb often contracts with a vowel following, and this contraction takes the accent. 16. Unlike many dialects, Lenje admits of many monosyllabic words, e. g. ma, ta, no, me, we, te, ndo, ku, &c. ... [Vocabulary preface, p. 72:] An accent (´) is written in some cases, where it falls in an unusual place.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page image we hold (p. 10, sec. 15) and scanned text; locator and the '15 vs 16' scanned note are correct. (2) The classification 'fixed penult' rests entirely on Madan 1908, a missionary practical handbook whose accent remark is impressionistic and pre-tonal ('prominence.. by a distinct stress' on other syllables is almost certainly lexical/grammatical H tone). (3) The only modern description, Kagaya 1987 (downloaded now, open), analyzes Lenje as a tone language (H/L/ultra-low, sentence-final falling tones, verb tone patterns) and says nothing about stress or penultimate prominence, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the penult coding; Hyman 2009 (held) notes that closely related Tonga lacks penultimate lengthening, which is a mild warning that a Botatwe 'penult accent' should not be assumed. No phonology/prosody study of Lenje was found in Glottolog, Crossref

sources.quote: p. 5: 'The tone carrier unit of this language is a vowel (described as V) or N of the prenasalized consonant NC. ... Tone is marked on the tone carrier unit. There is a high level tone ..., a low level tone (V, no mark) and an ultra-low level tone. Furthermore, there is a falling tone from high, a falling tone from low and a falling tone from ultra-low. The ultra-low level tone and these falling tones appear only at the sentence-final position. ... The tonal pattern of a word with two different series of high tones before and after a low tone(s) is found in predicate verbs but not in infinitiv
sources.locator: Part I 'An outline of Cilenje', sec. 1-3 'Tones and Their Descriptions' and 1-4 'Syllable Structure', p. 5 (PDF part 1, page 5); outline pp. 1-40 checked
sources.note: Only modern linguistic description of Lenje with a phonology outline (tone system, syllable structure, tonetic transcription of ~2000 items); our classification rests solely on a 1908 missionary handbook. downloaded now: establishes Lenje as tonal, silent on penult accent — supports reading Madan's 'distinct stress on another syllable' as high tone.
